name: Eisenmenger Syndrome

criteria.description: Presence of pulmonary arterial hypertension confirmed by right heart catheterization or echocardiography
Reversal of initial left-to-right cardiac shunt to a right-to-left or bidirectional shunt causing cyanosis
Underlying congenital heart defect with systemic-to-pulmonary shunting (e.g., ventricular septal defect, atrial septal defect, patent ductus arteriosus)
Clinical evidence of central cyanosis and digital clubbing
Symptoms of exertional dyspnea or fatigue

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of congenital heart defect with systemic-to-pulmonary shunting, pulmonary hypertension, and reversal of shunt direction causing cyanosis
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis is clinical supported by imaging and hemodynamic studies; exclusion of other causes of pulmonary hypertension is essential.

pathognomonic.notes: Bluish discoloration of lips, tongue, and mucous membranes
Detected by echocardiography or cardiac catheterization

common.notes: Shortness of breath on physical activity
Generalized tiredness and decreased exercise tolerance
Awareness of irregular or rapid heartbeat
Transient loss of consciousness due to hypoxia or arrhythmia
Coughing up blood due to pulmonary vascular rupture

occasional.notes: Non-specific chest discomfort or angina-like pain
Due to hypoxia or secondary polycythemia
Nosebleeds related to increased blood viscosity
Swelling due to right heart failure

rare.notes: Due to paradoxical embolism and septic emboli
Ischemic events from emboli passing through shunt
Blood in urine secondary to hyperviscosity or renal infarction

laboratory: Elevated hematocrit and hemoglobin due to secondary polycythemia
Elevated brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) in heart failure
imaging: Echocardiography demonstrating right-to-left shunt and pulmonary hypertension
Chest X-ray showing enlarged pulmonary arteries and right heart enlargement
Cardiac catheterization confirming elevated pulmonary artery pressures and shunt reversal
genetic: No specific genetic mutation; associated with congenital heart defects
other: Pulse oximetry showing decreased oxygen saturation
Electrocardiogram with right ventricular hypertrophy and strain patterns

distinguishingFeatures: Progressive pulmonary hypertension without shunt reversal
No initial left-to-right shunt with subsequent reversal
Different anatomical defects such as Tetralogy of Fallot

redFlags: Sudden worsening of cyanosis or hypoxemia
Signs of right heart failure such as peripheral edema and ascites
references: Galiè N, Humbert M, Vachiery JL, et al. 2015 ESC/ERS Guidelines for the diagnosis and treatment of pulmonary hypertension. Eur Heart J. 2016.
Beghetti M, Galie N. Eisenmenger syndrome a clinical perspective in a new therapeutic era of pulmonary arterial hypertension. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2009.
Warnes CA. The adult with Eisenmenger syndrome: current concepts. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2009.
